title: Real-World Applications of Generative AI
learning_outcomes: Explain education and personalized learning and how it connects to real-world applications of generative ai.
Apply business operations and customer support in the example and predict the output before running it.
Test one realistic edge case for real-world applications of generative ai and explain what the example does not prove.

content.intro: This lesson covers real-world applications of generative ai through 7 syllabus subtopics preserved from the supplied Generative AI curriculum. Start with what generative systems do, where they are useful, and why generated output needs review. Learn the vocabulary before choosing tools.
content.why_it_matters: Use education and personalized learning as a lens for understanding real-world applications of generative ai. Trace its inputs, the operation or decision it describes, the result a learner can observe, and the limitations that matter for the intended task. Confirm the idea with a small example and an explicit check rather than relying on fluent or plausible output.

items.title: Business operations and customer support
items.text: Use business operations and customer support to reason about behavior under real workloads, not just a successful local example. Measure latency and cost on representative requests, define operational limits and rollback options, and test what happens when dependencies slow down or fail.

content_blocks.title: Provider and version note
content_blocks.text: Model names, API payloads, supported modalities, quotas, pricing, and SDK behavior vary by provider and change over time. Treat linked official documentation as the authority for a live integration; examples here avoid hard-coded production model IDs and secrets.

content.task: Practice education and personalized learning within real-world applications of generative ai: use a small synthetic input, predict the result, run the example, then change one input to test an edge case. Record the expected result and one limitation.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example uses a clearly described, non-sensitive input.
Expected behavior and at least one edge/failure case are written down.
The learner checks the result against an explicit criterion and records limitations.
hints: Begin with a tiny input whose expected behavior you can explain before running it.
Change one variable at a time and retain a fixed baseline for comparison.
When a model or external service is involved, inspect evidence and errors; do not treat the model response as a trusted instruction.
content.expected_output: {'education': 'draft practice questions', 'support': 'summarize a ticket', 'software': 'explain a function'}

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming fluent or plausible output is necessarily correct.
common_mistakes.fix: Use evidence, schema checks, representative test cases, and human review for consequential results.

common_mistakes.mistake: Changing several inputs or parameters at once.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep a baseline and vary one factor at a time so the effect can be interpreted.

common_mistakes.mistake: Putting secrets or private source material in prompts, logs, or a public example.
common_mistakes.fix: Use synthetic data, server-side secret storage, data minimization, and reviewed retention rules.
